\label{thm:overview_main} 
{\rm (i)} The ambient part quantum $D$-module
of $X_W$ 
and the narrow part quantum $D$-module  
of $(\mathbb C^N, W, \boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ are analytically continued 
to each other\footnote
{See \S \ref{subsubsec:QDM} for the definition of 
the quantum $D$-modules. We mean by ``ambient part" 
the cohomology classes pulled back from the ambient 
space, see \S \ref{subsubsec:GW-statespace}; 
in FJRW side, this has a counterpart called 
``narrow part", see \S \ref{subsubsec:FJRW-statespace}. 
}, 
i.e.\ both of them are the restrictions of a global $D$-module over the 
K\"{a}hler moduli space $\mathcal{M}$.  

{\rm (ii)} The analytic continuation in {\rm (i)} 
matches up the $\widehat{\Gamma}$-integral structures  
on both quantum $D$-modules. 
Moreover, the induced isomorphism between the numerical $K$-groups 
of the categories of B-branes coincide with the one induced 
by the Orlov derived equivalence.
nodes.clean_text: (i) The ambient part quantum D-module of X_W and the narrow part quantum D-module of (mathbb C^N, W, boldsymbolmu_d) are analytically continued to each otherfootnote See S for the definition of the quantum D-modules. We mean by ``ambient part" the cohomology classes pulled back from the ambient space, see S ; in FJRW side, this has a counterpart called ``narrow part", see S . , i.e.\ both of them are the restrictions of a global D-module over the K\"ahler moduli space M. (ii) The analytic continuation in (i) matches up the widehatGamma-integral structures on both quantum D-modules. Moreover, the induced isomorphism between the numerical K-groups of the categories of B-branes coincide with the one induced by the Orlov derived equivalence.
nodes.label: thm:overview_main

nodes.name: Theorem \ref{thm:monodromyrep}
nodes.statement: (i) For each integer lin mathbb Z, there exists a path gamma_l from a neighbourhood of the large radius limit point to a neighbourhood of the LG point such that the analytic continuation along gamma_l^-1 is induced by the Orlov equivalence Phi_l. (ii) Let N'(X_W) be the subgroup of the numerical K-group of X_W consisting of K-classes whose Chern characters lie in the ambient cohomology H_amb(X_W) and let chi be the Euler pairing. The monodromy representation of the global D-module in Theorem \[ rho colon pi_1(M) to Aut(N'(X_W),chi) \] can be lifted to a group homomorphism \[ hatrho colon pi_1(M) to Auteq(D^b(X_W))/[2], \] where [2] is the 2-shift functor. The homomorphism hatrho sends a (clockwise) loop around the conifold point to the spherical twist by the structure sheaf.

The monodromy representation of the global D-module in Theorem \[ rho colon pi_1(M) to Aut(N'(X_W),chi) \] can be lifted to a group homomorphism \[ hatrho colon pi_1(M) to Auteq(D^b(X_W))/[2], \] where [2] is the 2-shift functor.

\label{thm:overview-autoeq}
{\rm (i)} For each integer $l\in \mathbb Z$, there exists a path 
$\gamma_l$ from a neighbourhood of the large radius limit point to 
a neighbourhood of the LG point 
such that the analytic continuation along $\gamma_l^{-1}$ 
is induced by the Orlov equivalence $\Phi_l$. 

{\rm (ii)} 
Let $N'(X_W)$ be the subgroup \eqref{eq:Nprime} of the 
numerical $K$-group of $X_W$ consisting of $K$-classes 
whose Chern characters lie in the ambient cohomology 
$H_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)$ 
and let $\chi$ be the Euler pairing. 
The monodromy representation of the 
global $D$-module in Theorem \ref{thm:overview_main}
\[
\rho \colon \pi_1(\mathcal{M}) \to \operatorname{Aut}(N'(X_W),\chi)
\]
can be lifted to a group homomorphism 
\[
\hat{\rho} \colon \pi_1(\mathcal{M})
\to \operatorname{Auteq}(D^b(X_W))/[2], 
\] 
where $[2]$ is the $2$-shift functor. 
The homomorphism $\hat{\rho}$ sends a (clockwise) loop around the conifold 
point to the spherical twist by the structure sheaf.

(ii) Let N'(X_W) be the subgroup of the numerical K-group of X_W consisting of K-classes whose Chern characters lie in the ambient cohomology H_amb(X_W) and let chi be the Euler pairing. The monodromy representation of the global D-module in Theorem \[ rho colon pi_1(M) to Aut(N'(X_W),chi) \] can be lifted to a group homomorphism \[ hatrho colon pi_1(M) to Auteq(D^b(X_W))/[2], \] where [2] is the 2-shift functor. nodes.statement: The definition of a W-structure originates from the Witten equation, which is a system of PDE for sections s_i in C^infty(C,L_i), i=1,dots, N: overlinepartial s_j + overlinepartial_j W(s_1,dots,s_N) = 0. The equation makes sense under and a suitable choice of a Hermitian metric on L_i (see ). When all the marked points correspond to the narrow sector, the zero sections are only possible solutions to the Witten equation and the FJRW invariant is the Euler class of the obstruction bundle over the moduli space of W-curves. We briefly review the general case.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:Wstr-origin} 
The definition \eqref{eq:W-str} of a $W$-structure 
originates from the Witten equation, 
which is a system of PDE for 
sections $s_i \in C^\infty(C,L_i)$, 
$i=1,\dots, N$: 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:WittenPDE}
\overline{\partial} s_j + \overline{\partial_j W(s_1,\dots,s_N)} = 0. 
\end{equation} 
The equation makes sense under \eqref{eq:W-str}  
and a suitable choice of a Hermitian metric on $L_i$ 
(see \cite{FJR:virt}). 
When all the marked points correspond to the narrow sector, 
the zero sections are only possible solutions to 
the Witten equation 
\cite[Theorem 3.3.8]{FJR:virt} 
and the FJRW invariant is the Euler class of the obstruction 
bundle over the moduli space of $W$-curves. We briefly review the general case.

The equation makes sense under and a suitable choice of a Hermitian metric on L_i (see ). When all the marked points correspond to the narrow sector, the zero sections are only possible solutions to the Witten equation and the FJRW invariant is the Euler class of the obstruction bundle over the moduli space of W-curves. We briefly review the general case.
nodes.label: rem:Wstr-origin

\label{lem:concave}
Suppose that $k_i+1 \in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$ for all $i$.
Then $H^0(C,L^{\otimes w_j})$ vanishes for all $j=1,\dots, N$ for  
$(C;\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n;L;\varphi)\in 
\operatorname{Spin}^d_{0,n}(k_1,\dots,k_n)$. 
In particular, the obstruction bundle  
$\bigoplus_{j=1}^N R^1\pi_* (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})$ 
over $\operatorname{Spin}^d_{0,n}(k_1,\dots,k_n)$ 
is locally free of rank $2 - N + \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^N \fracp{k_i q_j}$.

In particular, the obstruction bundle bigoplus_j=1^N R^1pi_* (L^otimes w_j) over Spin^d_0,n(k_1,dots,k_n) is locally free of rank 2 - N + sum_i=1^n sum_j=1^N fracpk_i q_j.
nodes.label: lem:concave

Then \[ p^* p_* (L^otimes w_j) = L^otimes w_j otimes O_Cleft( - sum_i=1^n d age_sigma_i (L^otimes w_j) sigma_i right) = L^otimes w_jotimes O_Cleft( - sum_i=1^n d fracp(k_i+1) q_j sigma_i right). \] Here we regard sigma_i as a stacky divisor of degree 1/d. Hence L' := (p^* p_* (L^otimes w_j))^otimes (q_j^-1) & = omega_logotimes O_Cleft( -sum_i=1^n d q_j^-1 fracp(k_i+1) q_jsigma_i right). Notice that q_j^-1 = d/w_j is an integer by the Gorenstein condition and q_j^-1 fracp(k_i+1) q_j ge 1 since k_i+1 in Nar. Hence L' is a subsheaf of the pull-back of omega_|C|. Note that H^0(|C|,omega_|C|)=0 since |C| is of genus zero. Hence H^0(C, L')=0 and thus H^0(C,p^* p_* (L^otimes w_j)) =0. This implies H^0(C, L^otimes w_j) =0. Finally, by Riemann-Roch , R^1 pi_* (L^otimes w_j) is locally free of rank -chi(L^otimes w_j) & = -1 - deg L^otimes w_j + sum_i=1^n age_sigma_i(L^otimes w_j) = -1 - (n-2)q_j + sum_i=1^n fracp(k_i+1)q_j \\ & = -1 + 2 q_j + sum_i=1^n fracpq_j k_i. The conclusion follows.

Let $p\colon C \to \overline{C}$ denote the map forgetting the 
stack-theoretic structures at all the markings 
(but not at the nodes). 
Then 
\[
p^* p_* (L^{\otimes w_j}) = L^{\otimes w_j} \otimes 
\mathcal{O}_C\left( - \sum_{i=1}^n 
d \operatorname{age}_{\sigma_i} (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}) \sigma_i \right) 
= L^{\otimes w_j}\otimes \mathcal{O}_C\left(
- \sum_{i=1}^n d \fracp{(k_i+1) q_j} \sigma_i \right). 
\]  
Here we regard $\sigma_i$ as a stacky divisor of degree $1/d$. 
Hence 
\begin{align*} 
L' := (p^* p_* (L^{\otimes w_j}))^{\otimes (q_j^{-1})}  
& = \omega_{\rm \log}\otimes \mathcal{O}_C\left(
-\sum_{i=1}^n d q_j^{-1} \fracp{(k_i+1) q_j}\sigma_i 
\right). 
\end{align*} 
Notice that $q_j^{-1} = d/w_j$ is an integer by the Gorenstein condition 
and $q_j^{-1} \fracp{(k_i+1) q_j} \ge 1$ since $k_i+1 \in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$. 
Hence $L'$ is a subsheaf of the pull-back of $\omega_{|C|}$. 
Note that $H^0(|C|,\omega_{|C|})=0$ since $|C|$ is of genus zero. 
Hence $H^0(C, L')=0$ 
and thus $H^0(C,p^* p_* (L^{\otimes w_j})) =0$. 
This implies $H^0(C, L^{\otimes w_j}) =0$. 
Finally, by Riemann-Roch \cite{AGV, Kawasaki, Toen}, 
$R^1 \pi_* (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})$ is locally free of rank 
\begin{align*} 
-\chi(L^{\otimes w_j}) & = 
-1 - \deg L^{\otimes w_j} + \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{age}_{\sigma_i}(L^{\otimes w_j}) 
=  
-1 - (n-2)q_j + \sum_{i=1}^n  \fracp{(k_i+1)q_j} \\ 
& = -1 + 2 q_j + \sum_{i=1}^n \fracp{q_j k_i}. 
\end{align*} 
The conclusion follows.

nodes.statement: Polishchuk and Vaintrob recently constructed a purely algebraic cohomological field theory of singularities based on matrix factorizations. They constructed a fundamental matrix factorization on the moduli space which plays the same role as the virtual fundamental class. The role of matrix factorizations in our paper is different from theirs, but it would be interesting to study the relationships.

nodes.statement: The FJRW and GW state spaces can be identified, up to Tate twist, with the relative Chen-Ruan cohomology (Chiodo-Nagel ): H(W,boldsymbolmu_d) & = H_CRleft( [mathbb C^N/boldsymbolmu_d], [W^-1(1)/boldsymbolmu_d]right) \\ H_CR(X_W) & = H_CR( O_mathbb P(underlinew)(-d), widetildeW^-1(1)). The first identification follows immediately from the definition. The second identification follows from the Thom isomorphism. Here widetildeWcolon O_mathbb P(underlinew)(-d) to mathbb C is the function in S . Note that the pairs (O_mathbb P(underlinew)(-d), widetildeW^-1(1)), ([mathbb C^N/boldsymbolmu_d], [W^-1(1)/boldsymbolmu_d]) are connected by a variation of GIT quotients. Chiodo-Ruan showed that there exists a bigraded isomorphism \[ H^p,q(W,boldsymbolmu_d) cong H^p,q_CR(X_W) \] which preserves the pairings on both sides. In this paper, we will construct a graded isomorphism (preserving the pairing) \[ H^p,p_nar(W,boldsymbolmu_d) cong H^p,p_amb(X_W) \] which depends on a point of the K\"ahler moduli space. (Note that the narrow/ambient part has no (p,q)-Hodge component with pneq q.) See Remark .
nodes.raw_latex:
The FJRW and GW state spaces 
can be identified, up to Tate twist, with 
the \emph{relative} Chen-Ruan cohomology 
(Chiodo-Nagel \cite{CN:CICY}): 
\begin{align*} 
H(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d) & = H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}\left(
[\mathbb C^N/\boldsymbol{\mu}_d], [W^{-1}(1)/\boldsymbol{\mu}_d]\right) \\ 
H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(X_W) & = H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(
\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P(\underline{w})}(-d), \widetilde{W}^{-1}(1)). 
\end{align*} 
The first identification follows immediately from the definition. 
The second identification follows from the Thom isomorphism.  
Here $\widetilde{W}\colon \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P(\underline{w})}(-d) \to \mathbb C$ is the 
function in \S \ref{subsec:overview}. 
Note that the pairs $(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P(\underline{w})}(-d), \widetilde{W}^{-1}(1))$, 
$([\mathbb C^N/\boldsymbol{\mu}_d], [W^{-1}(1)/\boldsymbol{\mu}_d])$ are connected
by a variation of GIT quotients. 
Chiodo-Ruan \cite{ChiR} showed that there 
exists a bigraded isomorphism 
\[
H^{p,q}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d) \cong H^{p,q}_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(X_W)
\]
which preserves the pairings on both sides. 
In this paper, we will construct a graded isomorphism 
(preserving the pairing) 
\[
H^{p,p}_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d) \cong 
H^{p,p}_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W) 
\]
which \emph{depends} on a point of the K\"{a}hler moduli space. 
(Note that the narrow/ambient part has no $(p,q)$-Hodge component 
with $p\neq q$.) See Remark \ref{rem:gradedisom}.

nodes.raw_latex:
Because of the deformation invariance (\cite[Theorem 1.2.5]{FJR:virt}, 
\cite[Theorem 3.4.2]{Chen-Ruan:GW})  
we can assume that $W$ is of Fermat type 
$W = x_1^{d/w_1} + \cdots + x_N^{d/w_N}$. 
Then the maximal diagonal group of symmetries preserving $W$ 
is given as 
$G_{\max} = 
\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\,|\, z_i^{d/w_i} =1\} 
\cong \boldsymbol{\mu}_{d/w_1} \times \cdots \times \boldsymbol{\mu}_{d/w_N}$. 
The $G_{\max}$-action on $\mathbb C^N$ naturally lifts to 
the state space $H$. 
We claim that $H'$ is the $G_{\max}$-invariant 
part of $H$: 
\begin{equation*} 
\label{eq:G_max-fixed}
H' = H^{G_{\max}} 
\end{equation*}
and that $H''$ is the sum of non-trivial 
irreducible $G_{\max}$-representations. 
The proposition follows from this claim and the 
$G_{\max}$-invariance of the correlator: 
\[
\corr{\tau_{b_1} (g\alpha_1), \dots
\tau_{b_n} (g\alpha_n), \tau_{c} (g\gamma)}_{0,n+1} 
= \corr{\tau_{b_1} (\alpha_1),\dots, 
\tau_{b_n} (\alpha_n), \tau_c(\gamma)}_{0,n+1}, 
\quad g\in G_{\max}. 
\]

First we show the claim for the FJRW state space.  
We use the description of $H(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)_k$ 
as the Jacobi space $\Omega(W_k)^{\boldsymbol{\mu}_d}$ 
given in \eqref{eq:FJRWstatespace_Jacobi} 
If $k\in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$, the sector $H(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)_k$ is 
obviously $G_{\max}$-invariant. 
Assume that $k\notin \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$. Then 
each element of $H(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)_k$ can be represented 
by a sum of monomial $N_k$-forms of the form 
$\prod_{k q_i \in \mathbb Z} (x_i^{a_i} d x_i)$ with 
$0\le a_i \le d/w_i-2$. 
But each summand spans a non-trivial irreducible 
$G_{\max}$-representations and the claim follows. 

Next we show the claim for the GW state space. 
Each twisted sector has a decomposition 
$H(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f \cap X_W) = H_{\operatorname{amb}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f \cap 
X_W) \oplus H_{\operatorname{pri}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f \cap X_W)$. 
It is obvious that $H_{\operatorname{amb}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f \cap X_W)$ 
is $G_{\max}$-invariant. The primitive part 
$H_{\operatorname{pri}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f\cap X_W)$ is isomorphic 
to $\operatorname{Gr}_{N_k}^{\marsfs{W}} H^{N_k-1}(W^{-1}(1))$ for $k=fd$ 
(see \cite[p.216]{Steenbrink}), 
which is $H(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)_k$ (see Appendix \ref{sec:proof-Jacobi}). 
Now the claim follows for the same reason as 
the previous paragraph, since $k=fd \notin \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:QDM}
Let $F = H' \times (U\times \mathbb C) \to U\times \mathbb C$ 
be the trivial vector bundle with fibre $H'$. 
Let $\nabla$ be the meromorphic 
flat connection (quantum connection) on $F$ 
\[
\nabla = \mathsf{d} + \frac{1}{z} \sum_{i=0}^r (T_i \bullet) \mathsf{d} t^i 
+\left( - \frac{1}{z}(E \bullet) + \operatorname{\mathsf{Gr}}
\right) \frac{\mathsf{d} z}{z} 
\]
which can be regarded as a map 
\[
\nabla \colon \mathcal{O}(F) \to \mathcal{O}(F)(U\times \{0\}) 
\otimes \left(
\pi^* \Omega_U^1 \oplus \mathcal{O}_{U\times \mathbb C} \frac{\mathsf{d} z}{z} 
\right). 
\]
Here $\mathcal{O}(F)(U\times \{0\})$ denotes the sheaf of 
holomorphic sections of $F$ with at most simple poles 
along $\{z=0\} = U\times \{0\}$. 
Let $P$ be an $\mathcal{O}_{U\times \mathbb C}$-bilinear pairing 
\[
(-)^* \mathcal{O}(F) \otimes \mathcal{O}(F) \to z^{\hat{c}} \mathcal{O}_{U\times \mathbb C} 
\]
defined by 
\[
P((-)^*s_1, s_2) 
:= (2\pi\mathtt{i} z)^{\hat{c}} (s_1(t,-z), s_2(t,z)). 
\]
Here $\hat{c} = \dim X_W = N-2$ and 
$(\cdot, \cdot)$ in the right-hand side 
denotes the standard pairing on the state 
space defined in \eqref{eq:FJRW-pairing} and 
\eqref{eq:GW-pairing}.   
The pairing satisfies 
\begin{align*} 
(-1)^{\hat{c}} P((-)^* s_1, s_2) & =  (-)^* P((-)^* s_2, s_1)  \\
\mathsf{d} P((-)^*s_1,s_2) & 
= P((-)^* \nabla s_1, s_2) + P((-)^* s_1,\nabla s_2). 
\end{align*} 
We call the tuple $(F,\nabla,P)$ 
\emph{the narrow part quantum $D$-module} 
$QDM_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ 
(in the case of FJRW theory) and 
\emph{the ambient part quantum $D$-module} 
$QDM_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)$ 
(in the case of GW theory).

gives rise to a variation of Hodge structure,

\] 
and the polarization 
\[

\left((-1)^{\deg/2} \alpha,\beta \right).
\]

For a $d$-spin structure $L\to C$ on a pointed orbicurve 
$(C,\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$,  
we have $\deg(L) - \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{age}_{\sigma_i}(L) \in \mathbb Z$ 
by Riemann-Roch for orbicurves \cite{AGV, Kawasaki, Toen}.  
Thus the moduli space $\operatorname{Spin}_{0,n}^d(k_1,\dots,k_n)$ is 
empty unless $2 + \sum_{i=1}^n k_i \equiv 0 \mod d$. 
Therefore we have 
\[
\corr{\tau_{b_1}(G(\phi_{k_1})),\dots,\tau_{b_n}(G(\phi_{k_n}))}
_{0,n}^{{\operatorname{FJRW}}} = e^{2(2\pi\mathtt{i})/d} 
\corr{\tau_{b_1}(\phi_{k_1}),\dots,\tau_{b_n}(\phi_{k_n})}
_{0,n}^{{\operatorname{FJRW}}} 
\]
for $k_1+1,\dots,k_n+1 \in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$. 
This fact and the formula \eqref{eq:pairing_narrow} 
of the pairing show that 
\[
G(\alpha_1) \bullet_{G(t)} G(\alpha_2) = G(\alpha_1 \bullet_t \alpha_2) 
\]
for $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in H'$. 
Here the subscripts of $\bullet$ 
denote the parameter of the quantum product. 
The statement follows easily from this.

\label{pro:Gamma-intstr-properties}
{\rm (1)} The $\widehat{\Gamma}$-integral structure is preserved under 
the Galois action, i.e.\ 
\begin{alignat*}{2}
e^{-2\pi\mathtt{i}/d} G \left( \mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{E})(G^{-1}(t),z) \right) 
& = \mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{E}(1))(t,z)  
& & \text{\rm for FJRW theory}; \\ 
\mathsf{d} G \left( \mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{E})(G^{-1}(t), z) \right) & = 
\mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{E}\otimes \mathcal{O}(-1))(t,z) \quad 
& & \text{\rm for GW theory},   
\end{alignat*} 
where $\mathcal{E}(1)$ is the shift of the grading of $\mathcal{E}$ by $1$. 
In particular, $F_\mathbb Z$ defines an integral structure 
on the quotient $(F,\nabla,P)/\langle G \rangle$. 

{\rm (2)} We have 
\begin{alignat*}{2}

\label{thm:main} 
There exists a locally free sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathcal{M} \times \mathbb C_z$ 
with a meromorphic flat connection $\nabla$ (with simple poles 
along $z=0$) 
\[
\nabla \colon \mathcal{F} \to 
\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{M}\times \{0\}) \otimes \Omega_{\mathcal{M}\times \mathbb C_z}^1, 
\]
a $\nabla$-flat, symmetric and non-degenerate pairing 
\[
P \colon (-)^*\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{F} \to z^{\hat{c}} \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}\times \mathbb C_z} 
\]
and a $\mathbb Z$-local subsystem $F_\mathbb Z$ of the same rank 
over $\mathcal{M}\times \mathbb C_z^\times$ 
\[
F_\mathbb Z \subset (\mathcal{F}|_{\mathcal{M} \times \mathbb C_z^\times})^\nabla 
\]
such that the following holds: 

{\rm (i)} For a small open neighbourhood 
$U_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}} = \{|u|<\epsilon\}\subset \mathcal{M}$ of the LG point, 
we have a mirror map $\tau_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}} \colon U_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}} \to 
H^2_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)/\langle G\rangle$ 
such that $\tau_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}} = -u \phi_1 + O(u^2)$ and 
\[
(\mathcal{F}, \nabla, (-1)^{N-1}P, F_\mathbb Z) \Bigr |_{U_{\operatorname{FJRW}} \times \mathbb C_z} 
\cong \tau_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}^* 
\left( QDM_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d) /\langle G\rangle \right),   
\]
where in the right-hand side appears 
the narrow part quantum $D$-module (Definition \ref{defn:QDM}) 
of $(\mathbb C^N, W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ equipped with the $\widehat{\Gamma}$-integral 
structure (Definition \ref{defn:intstr}) 
and $G$ is the Galois action (\S \ref{subsubsec:Galois}). 

{\rm (ii)} For a small open neighbourhood 
$U_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}} = \{|v|<\epsilon\}\subset \mathcal{M}$ 
of the large radius limit point, 
we have a mirror map 
$\tau_{\operatorname{_{GW}}} \colon U_\operatorname{\text{GW}} \to H^2_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)/\langle G\rangle$
such that $\tau_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}(v) = p \log v + O(v)$ and 
\[
(\mathcal{F}, \nabla, P, F_\mathbb Z) \Bigr |_{U_\operatorname{\text{GW}} \times \mathbb C_z} 
\cong \tau_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}^*\left( 
QDM_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)/\langle G\rangle \right),   
\] 
where in the right-hand side appears 
the ambient part quantum $D$-module of $X_W$ 
equipped with the $\widehat{\Gamma}$-integral structure
and $G$ is the Galois action.

\label{rem:gradedisom} 
Restricting the global $D$-module $(\mathcal{F},\nabla,P,F_\mathbb Z)$ 
to $z=1$, we obtain the analytic continuation between 
the narrow A-model VHS of $(\mathbb C^N,W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ 
and the ambient A-model VHS of $X_W$ in 
Remark \ref{rem:A-VHS}. 
The fibre $\mathcal{F}_{(x,1)}$ at $(x,1)\in \mathcal{M}\times \mathbb C_z$ has 
a well-defined filtration and a polarization 
\begin{align*} 
\marsfs{F}^{\, p} ( \mathcal{F}_{(x,1)}) & = 
\left\{v\in \mathcal{F}_{(x,1)} \;|\; s_v(z) 
\text{ has a pole of order $\le \hat{c}-p$ at $z=0$} 
\right\} \\ 
Q(v_1,v_2) & = P(s_{v_1}(-1), s_{v_2}(1)), \quad 
v_1,v_2 \in \mathcal{F}_{(x,1)}  
\end{align*} 
where $s_v(z) \in H^0(\mathbb C^\times_z, \mathcal{F}|_{\{t\}\times \mathbb C_z^\times})$ 
is a unique $\nabla$-flat section such that $s_v(1)=v$. 
The filtration and the polarization coincide with those 
of the A-model VHS near the respective limit point. 
By analytic continuation, we have an isomorphism 
of state spaces 
\[
\Theta(x) \colon (H_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d), \marsfs{F}^{\, p}_{\rm A}, Q_{\rm A}) 
\cong (H_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W), \marsfs{F}^{\, p}_{\rm A}, Q_{\rm A})  
\]
for a point $x$ on the universal cover $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$. 
Taking the associated graded vector space 
with respect to $\marsfs{F}^{\,\bullet}$,  
we can turn this into a graded isomorphism 
(preserving the polarization). 
Note that $\Theta$ does not map the identity to the identity

\label{thm:big} 
Assume that $X_W$ is a manifold. 

{\rm (i)} The ``big" quantum product of $(\mathbb C^N,W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$ 
on the narrow part 
and the ``big" quantum product of $X_W$ 
on the ambient part 
are convergent in the sense of \S \ref{subsubsec:convergence}. 

{\rm (ii)} 
The global $D$-module $(\mathcal{F},\nabla,P,F_\mathbb Z)$ 
in Theorem \ref{thm:main} can be extended to 
a $D$-module $(\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}},\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}},P^{\operatorname{ext}},F_\mathbb Z^{\operatorname{ext}})$ 
over a base $\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}\times \mathbb C_z$, 
where $\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}$ is a complex manifold 
of dimension $\operatorname{rank} \mathcal{F} = \dim H_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)$ which contains 
a Zariski open subset $\mathcal{M}'$ of $\mathcal{M}$ as a 
submanifold. 
The extended $D$-module is identified 
with the ``big" narrow/ambient part quantum $D$-module 
of FJRW/GW theory in a 
neighbourhood of $U_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}$ or $U_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}$.  

More precisely, there exists a locally free sheaf 
$\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}}$ over $\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}\times \mathbb C_z $
equipped with a meromorphic flat connection $\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}}$ 
(with poles of order two along $z=0$)
\[
\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}} \colon \mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}} \to \mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}}(\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}
\times \{0\}) \otimes \left (
\pi^* \Omega_{\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}}^1 
\oplus \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}} \times \mathbb C_z} \frac{\mathsf{d} z}{z} 
\right), 
\]
where $\pi \colon \mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}} \times \mathbb C_z \to \mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}$ 
is the projection, 
a $\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}}$-flat, symmetric and non-degenerate 
pairing 
\[
P^{\operatorname{ext}} \colon (-)^* \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{F} \to z^{\hat{c}} \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}} \times \mathbb C_z} 
\]
and a $\mathbb Z$-local subsystem $F^{\operatorname{ext}}_\mathbb Z$ of the same rank 
over $\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}} \times \mathbb C^\times_z$ 
\[
F^{\operatorname{ext}}_\mathbb Z \subset (\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}}|_{\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}\times \mathbb C^\times_z})^{\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}}} 
\]
such that the following holds: 
























\begin{itemize} 
\item $(\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}},\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}}, P^{\operatorname{ext}}, F_\mathbb Z^{\operatorname{ext}})|_{\mathcal{M}'} 
= (\mathcal{F},\nabla,P,F_\mathbb Z)|_{\mathcal{M}'}$; 





\item 
There exist open neighbourhoods  
$U_\heartsuit^{\operatorname{ext}}$ of $U_{\heartsuit}$ in $\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{ext}}$ 
and open embeddings 
\[
\tau^{{\operatorname{ext}}}_\heartsuit \colon 
U_\heartsuit^{\operatorname{ext}} \hookrightarrow H'_\heartsuit/\langle G\rangle, 
\quad \tau^{\operatorname{ext}}_{\heartsuit}|_{U_{\heartsuit}} = \tau_{\heartsuit}
\]
for $\heartsuit = \operatorname{\text{GW}}$ and ${\operatorname{FJRW}}$ 
such that we have isomorphisms  
\begin{align*} 
(\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}},\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}},(-1)^{N-1} P^{\operatorname{ext}}, F_\mathbb Z^{\operatorname{ext}}) 
|_{U^{\operatorname{ext}}_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}}  
& \cong {\tau^{{\operatorname{ext}}}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}}^*
(QDM_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)/\langle G\rangle) \\ 
(\mathcal{F}^{\operatorname{ext}},\nabla^{\operatorname{ext}},P^{\operatorname{ext}}, F_\mathbb Z^{\operatorname{ext}}) |_{U^{\operatorname{ext}}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}}  
& \cong {\tau^{{\operatorname{ext}}}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}}^*  
(QDM_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W) /\langle G \rangle). 
\end{align*} 
\end{itemize}

\gamma_{\operatorname{con}}^{-1} & \longmapsto \ & T_\mathcal{O} &

nodes.raw_latex:
The proof parallels the argument of 
\cite[Lemma 4.1.1]{ChiRquintic}.  
Let us compare $\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}$ and 
$\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}$ after push-forward 
via the morphism $p\colon \mathcal{C} \to \overline\mathcal{C}$ 
forgetting the stack-theoretic structure at the markings. 
We get\footnote
{To see this, use $p^* p_* \mathcal{E} = 
\mathcal{E} \otimes \mathcal{O}(-\sum_{i=1}^n d\operatorname{age}_{\mathcal{D}_i}(\mathcal{E})\mathcal{D}_i)$ 
for an invertible sheaf $\mathcal{E}$ on $\mathcal{C}$.} 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:allyouwanttoknow}
p_*(\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})=
p_* (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}) \otimes
\mathcal O\left(-{\textstyle{\sum}}_{i:(k_i+1){w_j}\in d\mathbb Z} \overline\mathcal{D}_i\right), 
\end{equation}
where $\overline\mathcal{D}_i \subset \overline\mathcal{C}$ is the divisor supported 
on the $i$th coarse marking.  
Therefore, if $(k_i+1){w_j}\not \in d\mathbb Z$ for all $i$, we have
$R^{1}\pi_* (\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})=R^{1}\pi_* (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})$. 
This shows the second claim above. 























The vanishing condition in the statement holds 
when $(k_i + 1) w_j \in d \mathbb Z$ for some $1\le i\le n$ and 
some $1\le j\le N$. 
This simply means that $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}|_{\mathcal{D}_i}$ is 
pulled back from the coarse divisor $\overline\mathcal{D}_i$. 
On the other hand $\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}$ is a root of 
$\omega_{\log}$ and $\omega_{\log}|_{\mathcal{D}_i} \cong \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{D}_i}$ 
via the residue map. 
Therefore, $c_1(\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j}|_{\mathcal{D}_i})=0$ and 
hence $c_1(p_* (\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})|_{\overline\mathcal{D}_i})=0$ 
in the rational cohomology group. 

Set $\mathcal T = p_*(\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})$. 
From \eqref{eq:allyouwanttoknow}, 
$\mathcal T(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)|_{\overline\mathcal{D}_i} 
= p_*(\mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})|_{\overline\mathcal{D}_i}$ has 
vanishing first Chern class. 
Write the exact sequence 
\[
\begin{CD}
0@>>> \mathcal T @>>> \mathcal T (\overline\mathcal{D}_{i}) @>>> \mathcal T (\overline\mathcal{D}_{i})|_{\overline\mathcal{D}_{i}}
@>>> 0 
\end{CD}
\]
and the induced exact sequence of vector bundles 
\begin{equation}
\begin{CD} 
\label{eq:longexact}
0 @>>> \overline\pi_* \left( \mathcal T (\overline\mathcal{D}_{i})\rest{\overline\mathcal{D}_{i}} \right) 
@>>> R^1\overline\pi_* \mathcal T 
@>>> R^1\overline\pi_* \mathcal T (\overline\mathcal{D}_{i}) @>>> 0.   
\end{CD}
\end{equation} 
The vanishing ${c}_{\mathrm{top}} (R^1 \pi_* (\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})) 
={c}_{\mathrm{top}} (R^1\overline\pi_* \mathcal T)= 0$ 
follows from $c_1(\mathcal T (\overline\mathcal{D}_{i})\rest{\overline\mathcal{D}_{i}})=0$. 
Note that, in order to get \eqref{eq:longexact}, 
we need to show that $\mathcal T(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)$ has 
only trivial sections on each fibre $\overline{C}$ of $\overline\mathcal{C}$. 
For $a = d/w_j$, we find that 
$\mathcal T(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)^{\otimes a} \cong 
\overline\omega(\overline\mathcal{D}_i -\sum_{l\neq i} a \fracp{k_l/a} \overline\mathcal{D}_l)$ 
which is a subsheaf of $\overline\omega(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)$. 
It is easy to see that 
$H^0(\overline{C},\overline\omega(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)|_{\overline{C}})=0$ 
for a genus zero curve $\overline{C}$ by induction on 
the components (see \cite{ChiRquintic}).  
Therefore $H^0(\overline{C}, \mathcal T(\overline\mathcal{D}_i)|_{\overline{C}})=0$.

nodes.name: Givental's symplectic space
nodes.statement: Givental's symplectic space is the space \[ H := H_ext otimes K\z,z^-1\ \] equipped with the symplectic form \[ Omega^s(f_1,f_2)= Res_z=0 (f_1(-z),f_2(z))_s dz. \] The space H has a standard polarization H = H_+ oplus H_-, where H_+ = H_ext otimes K\z\, H_- = H_ext otimes z^-1 K \z^-1\ are isotropic subspaces of H. This polarization allows us to identify H with the total space of the cotangent bundle of H_+.
nodes.raw_latex:
Givental's symplectic space is the space 
\[
\mathcal{H} := H_{\operatorname{ext}} \otimes K\{z,z^{-1}\} 
\]
equipped with the symplectic form 
\[
\Omega^{\mathbf{s}}(f_1,f_2)= 
\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} (f_1(-z),f_2(z))_{\mathbf{s}} dz. 
\]
The space $\mathcal{H}$ has a standard polarization  
$\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_+ \oplus \mathcal{H}_-$, 
where $\mathcal{H}_{+} = H_{\operatorname{ext}} \otimes K\{z\}$, 
$\mathcal{H}_- = H_{\operatorname{ext}} \otimes z^{-1} K \{z^{-1}\}$ 
are isotropic subspaces of $\mathcal{H}$. 
This polarization allows us to identify 
$\mathcal{H}$ with the total space of 
the cotangent bundle of $\mathcal{H}_+$.

nodes.statement: Consider the universal characteristic class of the extended obstruction K-class: e(s)=expleft(sum_1le jle N sum_l=0^infty s_l^(j) ch_l (mathbb R pi_* widetilde L^otimes w_j)right) in H^*(Spin^d_0,n(k_1,dots,k_n);mathbb C)otimes K and define the twisted FJRW invariants as corrtau_b_1(phi_k_1),dots,tau_b_n(phi_k_n) _0,n^s=int_[Spin^d_0,n(k_1,dots,k_n)] left(prod_i=1^n psi_i^b_iright) cup e(s). nodes.raw_latex:
We relate the variables $\{t_b^k\}$ of $\mathbf{F}^\mathbf{s}_0$ 
and the co-ordinates $\{q_b^k\}$ on $\mathcal{H}_+$ 
by the following \emph{dilaton shift}: 
\[
q_b^k = - \delta_b^1 \delta^k_0 + t_b^k. 
\]
Then $\mathbf{F}_0^\mathbf{s}$ can be regarded as a function defined on 
a formal neighbourhood of $-z \phi_0 \in \mathcal{H}_+$. 
The graph of $\mathsf{d}\mathbf{F}_0^{\mathbf{s}}$ defines a Lagrangian 
submanifold of $(\mathcal{H},\Omega^\mathbf{s})$: 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:Lag-cone}
\mathcal{L}^{\mathbf{s}}:=\left\{ \mathbf{q} +\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{H} \,\Big |\, 
p_{b,k} = \parfrac{\mathbf{F}_0^{\mathbf{s}}}{q_b^k}, \ b\ge 0, 0\le k\le d-1 
\right \}.
\end{equation} 
The submanifold $\mathcal{L}^\mathbf{s}$ 
can be defined as a formal scheme over $K$. 
See \cite[Appendix B]{CCIT:computing}.

The discussion here is parallel to 
\cite[Theorem 4.8]{CCIT:computing} 
and \cite[Theorem 4.1.6]{ChiRquintic}. 
We give a sketch of the proof 
and leave the details to the reader. 


Introduce a function 
\begin{eqnarray*}
G^{(j)}_y(x,z)=\sum_{m,l\ge 0}
s^{(j)}_{l+m-1}\frac{B_m(y)}{m!}\frac{x^l}{l!}z^{m-1}, \quad 
j=1,\dots, N 
\end{eqnarray*}
with $s^{(j)}_{-1}=0$.
Set $D := \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} k t^k (\partial/\partial t^k)$. 
Givental's geometric properties for the cone $\mathcal{L}^{\rm un}$ 
yield the following fact (see 
\cite[Eqn (14)]{CCIT:computing} and 
\cite[Lemma 4.1.10]{ChiRquintic}): 











\begin{lem} 
\label{lem:diffop-applied} 
The family $t\mapsto \exp(-\sum_{j=1}^N 
G_{0}^{(j)}(zq_j D+zq_j,z))J^{\rm un}(t,-z)$ lies on $\mathcal{L}^{{\rm un}}$.\qed
\end{lem}












The conclusion of Theorem \ref{thm:I_is_on_the_cone} follows from 
Theorem \ref{thm:symplectictrans}: we apply the symplectic 
transformation $\Delta \colon (\mathcal{H},\Omega^{\rm un}) \to (\mathcal{H},\Omega^\mathbf{s})$ 
in \eqref{eq:transf} to the family in Lemma \ref{lem:diffop-applied}. 
Note that we have 
\[
\Delta = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{d-1} 
\exp \left( \sum_{j=1}^N G_{\fracp{iq_j}+q_j}^{(j)}(0,z) 
\right) 
= \bigoplus_{i=0}^{d-1} 
\exp \left( \sum_{j=1}^N G_0^{(j)}\left( (\fracp{iq_j} +q_j)z, z 
\right) \right) 
\]
where we used 
$G^{(j)}_y(x,z) = G^{(j)}_0(x + yz, z)$ 
in the second equality. 
Using the identity 
\[
G^{(j)}_0(x+z,z)=G^{(j)}_0(x,z)+\mathbf{s}^{(j)}(x) 
\]
we can easily check that 
\[
I^\mathbf{s}(t,-z) = \Delta \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^N 
G_0^{(j)}(zq_j D+zq_j,z)\right)J^{\rm un}(t,-z). 
\]
Theorem \ref{thm:symplectictrans} and Lemma \ref{lem:diffop-applied} 
show that $I^\mathbf{s}(t,-z)$ is on the cone $\mathcal{L}^{\mathbf{s}}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
Because of the problem we discussed in Remark \ref{rem:loglambda}, 
we use another specialization 
$s^{(j)}_l=\overline{s}^{(j)}_l$, where 
\[
\overline{s}^{(j)}_l := 
\begin{cases} 
0 & l =0; \\ 
(l-1)! (-\lambda_j)^{-l} & l\ge 0.
\end{cases} 
\]
This specialization yields $\exp(-\overline{\mathbf{s}}^{(j)}(x)) = 1 + x/\lambda_j$. 
It defines a well-defined homomorphism 
$K \to \mathbb C[\![\lambda^{-1}]\!] := 
\mathbb C[\![\lambda_1^{-1},\dots,\lambda_N^{-1}]\!]$ 
and the characteristic class: 
\[ 
e(\overline{\mathbf{s}}) = 
\left(\prod_{j=1}^N \lambda_j^{-r_j} \right)   
e_T\left(\bigoplus_{j=1}^N 
R^1\pi_*(\widetilde \mathcal{L}^{\otimes w_j})\right). 
\]
The Lagrangian cone $\mathcal{L}^{\overline{\mathbf{s}}}$ 
can be defined as a formal scheme over 
$\mathbb C[\![\lambda^{-1}]\!]$ 
and $I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(t,-z)$ is lying on $\mathcal{L}^{\overline{\mathbf{s}}}$ 
by Theorem \ref{thm:I_is_on_the_cone}. 
After some computation, we find that 
$J^{\rm tw}$ and $I^{\rm tw}$ are related to 
$J^{\overline\mathbf{s}}$ and $I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}$ as 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:tw-sbar}
\begin{split}  
J^{{\rm tw}}(t,z;\lambda) & = 
R(\lambda) 
J^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(R(\lambda)^{-1}t,z;\lambda) \\
I^{{\rm tw}}(u,z;\lambda) & =  R(\lambda) 
u I^{\overline{\mathbf{s}}}\left(- u R(\lambda)^{-1}\phi_1, z \right)
\end{split} 
\end{align} 
where $R(\lambda) \colon H_{\operatorname{ext}} \to H_{\operatorname{ext}}$ is 
defined by $R(\lambda)\phi_h = 
(\prod_{j=1}^N \lambda_j^{-\fracp{hq_j}}) \phi_h$.  
It is also easy to check that $I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(-u\phi_1,z)$ 
has the asymptotics 
\[
I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(-u\phi_1, z) = z \overline{F}(u;\lambda) \phi_0 + \overline{G}(u;\lambda) + O(z^{-1}) 
\]
for a scalar valued function $\overline{F} = 1 + O(u)$ 
and an $H_{\operatorname{ext}}^{\le 2}$-valued function $\overline{G}$. 
Here the functions $F$, $G$ appearing in 
\eqref{eq:FandG} are related to $\overline{F}$, 
$\overline{G}$ as 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:F-G-ovF-ovG}
F(u) = u \overline{F}(\lambda^q u;\lambda), \quad 
G(u;\lambda) = u R(\lambda) \overline{G}(\lambda^{q} u;\lambda) 
\end{equation} 
with $\lambda^q = \prod_{j=1}^N \lambda_j^{q_j}$. 
Because $\mathcal{L}^{\overline\mathbf{s}}$ is a cone and $I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(-u\phi_1,-z)$ 
is on $\mathcal{L}^{\overline\mathbf{s}}$, we have 
(we regard $I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(-u\phi_1,-z)$ as a 
$\mathbb C[\![\lambda^{-1}]\!][\![u]\!]$-valued 
point on $\mathcal{L}^{\overline\mathbf{s}}$ and apply 
\cite[Proposition B2]{CCIT:computing}): 
\[
\frac{1}{\overline{F}(u;\lambda)} 
I^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(-u\phi_1,-z) 
= -z \phi_0 + \frac{\overline{G}(u;\lambda)}{\overline{F}(u;\lambda)}   
+ O (z^{-1}) \in \mathcal{L}^{\overline\mathbf{s}}. 
\]
By the characterization \eqref{eq:charactJ} of the $J$-function, 
this coincides with $J^{\overline\mathbf{s}}(\overline{G}(u;\lambda)/\overline{F}(u;\lambda),-z)$. 
The conclusion follows from this and  
the relations \eqref{eq:tw-sbar}, \eqref{eq:F-G-ovF-ovG}.

\label{defn:grMFjsigma}
A \emph{graded matrix factorization} of $W$ 
is a collection $(E^i,\delta_i)_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ 
of finitely generated graded free $R$-modules $E^i$ 
and degree-zero homomorphisms 
$\delta_i\in \operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{gr-}}R}(E^i,E^{i+1})$ 


\[
\begin{CD} 
\cdots @>{\delta_{-1}}>> E^0 @>{\delta_0}>> E^1 
@>{\delta_1}>> E^2 
@>{\delta_2}>> E^3 @>{\delta_3}>> \cdots 
\end{CD}    
\]






such that it is 2-periodic up to the shift of grading 
\[ 
E^{i+2}=E^i(d), \quad \delta_{i+2}=\delta_i(d)
\]
and that 
$\delta_{i+1}\circ \delta_{i} = 
W \cdot \operatorname{id}_{E^i}\colon E^i\to E^{i+2} = E^i(d)$ for all $i$.   
This is equivalent to the data $E^0$, $E^1$, 
$\delta_0\in \operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{gr-}}R}(E^0,E^1)$, 
$\delta_1\in\operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{gr-}}R}(E^1,E^0(d))$ 
such that $\delta_1\circ\delta_0=W\cdot \operatorname{id}_{E^0}$ 
and $\delta_0(d) \circ \delta_1=W\cdot \operatorname{id}_{E^1}$. 
These data are denoted also by $(E,\delta_E)$, 
where 
\[
E:= E^0 \oplus E^1, \quad 
\delta_E := 
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & \delta_1 \\ 
\delta_0 & 0 
\end{pmatrix} \colon E \to E \quad 
\text{satisfying} \quad \delta_E^2 = W \cdot \operatorname{id}_E. 
\]

These objects form a dg category as follows.

Consider the graded matrix factorizations 
$\overline{E}=(E^i,\delta_{i})_{i\in \mathbb Z}$ and 
$\overline{F}=(F^i,\delta'_{i})_{i\in \mathbb Z}$; 
the space of homomorphisms is defined to be 
the $\mathbb Z$-graded vector space 
\[
\operatorname{\mathsf{Hom}}^\bullet(\overline{E},\overline{F}) 
= \left\{ (f_n)_{n\in \mathbb Z} \,\Big|\, f_n\in 
\operatorname{Hom}_{{\operatorname{gr-}}R}(E^n,F^{n+\bullet}), \, 
f_{n+2} = f_n(d) \right\} 
\] 
equipped with the differential 
\[
(\mathsf{d} f)_n = \delta'_{n+\bullet} \circ f_n - (-1)^{\bullet}
f_{n+1} \circ \delta_{n}, \quad 
f\in \operatorname{\mathsf{Hom}}^\bullet(\overline{E},\overline{F}). 
\]
The homotopy category of the above 
dg category is denoted by $\operatorname{{MF}}^{\rm gr}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}_d}(W)$. 

It is a triangulated category.

The lower index in the notation $\operatorname{{MF}}^{\rm gr}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}_d}(W)$ 
emphasizes the fact that a graded matrix factorization  
is automatically $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-equivariant. 
The $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-action on $R$ is defined by 
$\zeta \cdot x_i = \zeta^{-w_i} x_i$, where 
$\zeta = \exp(2\pi\mathtt{i}/d)\in \boldsymbol{\mu}_d$. 
For a graded matrix factorization 
$\overline{E} = (E^i,\delta_{i})_{i\in \mathbb Z}$,  
we define the $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-action on $E^i$ by 
$\zeta \cdot e = \zeta^{-n} e$ for $e\in (E^i)_n$. 
Then the $R$-module $E^i$ is $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-linearized 
and $\delta_{i}$ is $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-equivariant.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:gradedKoszul-MF}
Suppose that $W$ is of the form 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:decomposition}
W=\sum_{i=1}^{N} a_ib_i 
\end{equation}
for homogeneous elements $a_i,b_i\in R$ such 
that $\deg(a_i) + \deg (b_i) = d$. 
Let $V$ be the graded vector space 
$\bigoplus_{i=1}^{N}  \mathbb C e_i$ with 
$\deg(e_i)=-\deg(a_i)$. 

For $q\in \mathbb Z$, the \emph{graded Koszul matrix factorization} 
$\{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_q$ is defined by the data 
\[
E^i= \bigoplus_{\substack{{k=0,\dots, N}\\ {k\equiv i\, (2)}}}
R\otimes \Bigl(\bigwedge^{k} V\Bigr) 
\left(\tfrac{d(i-k)}{2}+q\right), \quad 
\delta_i = \delta'_{\underline{a}} + \delta''_{\underline{b}} \colon 
E^i \to E^{i+1}, \quad i\in \mathbb Z, 
\]
where $\delta'_{\underline{a}}$, $\delta''_{\underline{b}}$ 
are the Koszul differentials: 
\[
\delta'_{\underline{a}} = \sum_{j=1}^N a_j e_j\wedge, \quad 
\delta''_{\underline{b}} = \sum_{j=1}^N b_j \iota(e^*_j).  
\]
Observe that the grading is shifted so that 
the map $\delta_i$ preserves the degree. 
Note also that $\{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_q = \{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_0(q)$.

\label{exa:ch-Koszul} 
For a general weighted homogeneous polynomial $W$, 
we can write $W = \sum_{j=1}^N a_j b_j$ 
with $a_j = q_j \partial_j W$, $b_j = x_j$ ($q_j := w_j/d$). 
The Chern character of the graded Koszul matrix factorization 
$\{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_q$ of $W$ is supported on the narrow sector. 
In fact, by a direct calculation, 





we obtain  
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:chernbrane}
{\rm ch}(\{\underline{a}, \underline{b}\}_q ) = 
\bigoplus_{k\in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}} 
\zeta^{qk}\left( 
\prod_{j=1}^{N}(1-\zeta^{-w_j k})
\right)  \phi_{k-1}. 
\end{equation}
See \cite[Proposition 4.3.4]{PVmf} where 
$\{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_0$ is denoted by $k^{\rm st}$. 
(The case $q\neq 0$ follows from the case with $q=0$ since 
$q$ is just a shift the grading.) 
These Chern characters span the narrow part $H_{\operatorname{nar}}(W,\boldsymbol{\mu}_d)$.

nodes.statement: Because Polishchuk-Vaintrob considered the G-equivariant (ungraded) matrix factorizations over the ring of formal power series, we need check that the Euler characteristic does not change under the base change from the polynomial ring to the formal power series ring for graded matrix factorizations. Set widehatR =mathbb C[\![x_1,dots,x_N]\!]. Let (E,delta_E), (F,delta_F) be graded matrix factorizations. Let (widehatE,hatdelta_E) = (E,delta_E) otimes_R widehatR, (widehatF,hatdelta_F) = (F,delta_F)otimes_R widehatR be boldsymbolmu_d-equivariant matrix factorizations over widehatR without the mathbb Z-grading. We have the identification as mathbb Z/2-graded complexes: \[ Hom^sigma left((widehatE,hatdelta_E),(widehatF,hatdelta_F) right) = mathbinwidehatbigoplus_j equiv sigma\, (2) Hom^j((E,delta_E),(F,delta_F)), sigma in mathbb Z/2, \] where the completed direct sum consists of arbitrary sequences of homomorphisms bounded in the negative direction. Hence the cohomology is again the completed direct sum of the cohomology H^j(Hom^bullet((E,delta_E),(F,delta_F))). The HRR for the left-hand side implies the finite-dimensionality and the boundedness of the cohomology of the right-hand side, and the HRR for the right-hand side as well.

Because Polishchuk-Vaintrob considered the $G$-equivariant 
(ungraded) matrix factorizations over the ring of formal power series,   
we need check that the Euler characteristic does 
not change under the base change from the polynomial 
ring to the formal power series ring for \emph{graded} 
matrix factorizations. 
Set $\widehat{R} =\mathbb C[\![x_1,\dots,x_N]\!]$. 
Let  $(E,\delta_E), (F,\delta_F)$ be graded matrix factorizations.  

Let $(\widehat{E},\hat{\delta}_E) = (E,\delta_E) \otimes_R \widehat{R}$, 
$(\widehat{F},\hat{\delta}_F) = (F,\delta_F)\otimes_R \widehat{R}$ 
be $\boldsymbol{\mu}_d$-equivariant matrix factorizations over $\widehat{R}$ 
without the $\mathbb Z$-grading. 
We have the identification as $\mathbb Z/2$-graded 
complexes: 
\[
\operatorname{\mathsf{Hom}}^\sigma \left((\widehat{E},\hat{\delta}_E),(\widehat{F},\hat{\delta}_F) \right) = 
\mathbin{\widehat\bigoplus}_{j \equiv \sigma\, (2)} 
\operatorname{\mathsf{Hom}}^j((E,\delta_E),(F,\delta_F)), \quad 
\sigma \in \mathbb Z/2, 
\]
where the completed direct sum consists of 
arbitrary sequences of homomorphisms  
bounded in the negative direction. 
Hence the cohomology is again the completed 
direct sum of the cohomology $H^j(\operatorname{\mathsf{Hom}}^\bullet((E,\delta_E),(F,\delta_F)))$. 
The HRR for the left-hand side 
implies the finite-dimensionality and the boundedness 
of the cohomology of the right-hand side, and 
the HRR for the right-hand side as well.

for $l\in \mathbb Z$ assigns to

Write $(E^i, \delta_i)_{i\in \mathbb Z} = \{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_q$. 
Let us consider $E^i\otimes_R S$
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:parity}
\bigoplus_{r\in \mathbb Z\mid r\equiv i\, (2)} 
S\otimes \Bigl(\bigwedge^{r} V \Bigr) 
\left(\textstyle \frac{d(i-r)}2+q\right). 
\end{equation}
where $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^N \mathbb C e_j$ with 
$\deg (e_j) = -\deg (a_j) = w_j -d$.  
Each summand is of the form 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:terms}
\bigoplus_{{j_1<\dots<j_r}}
S\left( \textstyle - \sum_{a=1}^r \deg(e_{j_a}) + \frac{d(i-r)}2 +q \right) 
= \bigoplus_{{j_1<\dots<j_r}}
S\left(\textstyle -\sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a}+\frac{d(i+r)}2 +q \right). 
\end{equation}

By Proposition \ref{pro:Orlovexplicit} and 
Remark \ref{rem:rightsemiinf} 
we can regard the image via $\Phi_l$ of 
the Koszul matrix factorization $\{\underline{a},\underline{b}\}_q$ 
as the (complementary) right semiinfinite complex 
$(L_l^c)^{\bullet} [1]$. 
The terms $S(h)$ appearing in the above formula 
contribute to $L_l^c$ if and only if $h\ge l$; 
therefore we consider the inequality
\begin{equation*}

h=-\sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a}+ \frac{i+r}{2}d + q \ge l, 
\end{equation*} 
which can be rewritten as (using $q- l = td +m$) 
\[
m +t d +  \frac{i+r}{2} d
\ge \sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a}.
\]
Since $\sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a}$ lies in $\{0,\dots,d\}$ 
by the CY condition $d=\sum_{j=1}^N w_j$,  
we deduce that $h\ge l$ 
if and only if either we have 
$(i+r)/2 > - t$ 
(note $i+r$ is even by \eqref{eq:parity}) 
or we have $m \ge \sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a}$ 
alongside with $({i+r})/2 =-t$. 

Let us consider all terms of \eqref{eq:terms} 
for which $(i+r)/2> -t$. 
Then, the summand of \eqref{eq:terms} 
attached to $j_1<\dots<j_r$ is of the form 
$S(l+n-\sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a})$ with $n\ge d$. 
Such summands with fixed $n$ 
form an exact sequence $\mathcal{E}_n^\bullet$ on $X_W$
\begin{multline}
\label{eq:exactseq}
\mathcal{E}_n^\bullet: \quad 
\mathcal O(l+n)\overset{\delta_{\underline{b}}''}
\longleftarrow \bigoplus_j \mathcal O(l+n-w_j)
\overset{\delta''_{\underline{b}}}\longleftarrow 
\bigoplus_{j_1<j_2}\mathcal O(l+n-w_{j_1}-w_{j_2})
\overset{\delta''_{\underline{b}}}\longleftarrow  \cdots \\ 
\overset{\delta''_{\underline{b}}}{\longleftarrow} 
\bigoplus_j \mathcal O\left( l + n -\textstyle\sum_{j'\neq j} w_{j'}\right)
\overset{\delta''_{\underline{b}}}\longleftarrow  \mathcal O(l +n-d)
\end{multline} 
where we wrote $\mathcal O(h)$ for $S(h)$ 
following Proposition \ref{pro:Orlovexplicit}. 
Therefore, all together, the sum  
\[ 

\bigoplus_{\substack{r\equiv i \, (2) \\ 
(i+r)/2 > -t }} 
S\otimes \Bigl( \bigwedge^r V\Bigr) \left(  
\textstyle \frac{d(i-r)}{2} +q \right) 
\] 
gives an acyclic subcomplex of $(L^{c}_l)^\bullet$. 
It is acyclic because it can be written 
as a successive extension by the 
acyclic complexes $\mathcal{E}_n^\bullet$ 
of a complex supported on arbitrarily 
high homological degrees.  

The quotient of $(L^c_l)^\bullet$ 
by this acyclic subcomplex consists of 
terms of \eqref{eq:terms} 
with $(i+r)/2 =-t$ 
and $\sum_{a=1}^r w_{j_a} \le m$. 
The conclusion follows. (Recall that 
we need to take the shift $(L^c_l)^\bullet[1]$ by 1.)

We take the Taylor expansion of the expression \eqref{eq:U} 
in $p$ first and check if the expansion are regular at $\xi=0$ 
when evaluated in $H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w}))$.  

If $k\in \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$, or equivalently $\fracp{k/d} \notin \mathfrak{F}$, 
there exists no $f\in \mathfrak{F}$ such that $\zeta^k e^{2\pi\mathtt{i} \overline{f}}=1$. 
Therefore \eqref{eq:U} is regular 
at $(p,\xi)=(0,0)$ 
and the conclusion follows. 

If $k\notin \operatorname{\mathsf{Nar}}$, 
\eqref{eq:U} is not regular at $(p,\xi)=(0,0)$. 
The only non-regular term in \eqref{eq:U} is the one with 
$f = \fracp{k/d}$ (in this case $\zeta^k e^{2\pi\mathtt{i} \overline{f}} =1$). 
We compute the Taylor expansion in $p$ 
of such term. 
By an elementary computation, we have 
\begin{align*} 
\frac{1}{e^{p+\frac{2\pi\mathtt{i}\xi}{d}} -1} 



& = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \beta_n(\xi)  p^n, \quad 
\beta_n(\xi) = (-1)^n 
\left(\frac{2\pi\mathtt{i}\xi}{d}\right)^{-n-1} + O(\xi^{-n}).  
\end{align*} 
When evaluated in the cohomology group $H(\mathbb P(\underline{w})_f)$, 
this Taylor series is truncated at $n=\dim \mathbb P(\underline{w})_f 
= N_k-1$ 
(where we used $f = \fracp{k/d}$). 
Therefore the factor $\prod_{j:kq_j \in \mathbb Z} (-q_j \xi)$ 
cancels all the negative powers of $\xi$ in $\beta_n$. 
Hence $\mathbb U^{\rm tw}_l(\phi_{k-1})$ is regular at $\xi=0$ 
and the conclusion follows.

Note that $(1/d)\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \zeta^{qk}$ 
equals $1$ if $q\in d\mathbb Z$ and $0$ otherwise. 
Thus we have 
\[
\frac{1}{d} \sum_{k=0}^{d-1}
\frac{\zeta^{kj}}{\zeta^ky-1}= 
-\frac{1}{d} 
\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} 
\sum_{n=0}^\infty 
(\zeta^{k})^{j+n} y^n 
=- 
\sum_{n\ge 0: j+n\in d\mathbb Z} y^n 
\]
The lemma follows.

A multi-generated hypergeometric system similar to $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ 
above appeared in the recent work of Borisov-Horja 
\cite{Borisov-Horja:BB} 
(also will appear in Coates-Corti-Iritani-Tseng \cite{CCIT:toric}). 
The $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw}$-submodule $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw} \Delta_0$ of 
$\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ generated by $\triangle_0$ coincides with 
$\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ at the generic point (Lemma \ref{lem:almostgenerate}),  
but not everywhere (for instance along $z=\lambda=0$). 
A closely related multi-generation phenomena 
of quantum cohomology was observed by 
Guest-Sakai \cite{Guest-Sakai} for a Fano hypersurface in $\mathbb P(\underline{w})$. 
It was shown in \cite{Iritani:period} that 
the quantum $D$-module of a toric Calabi-Yau hypersurface 
can be described by a multi-GKZ system.

Let x_0,dots,x_N be mirror mathbb C^times-variables subject to the relation \[ x_0^-d x_1^w_1 cdots x_N^w_N = v. \] The mirror potential W_lambda is defined by \[ W_lambda = x_1 + cdots + x_N - x_0 + lambdalog x_0. \] Then the integrals \[ I_nu(v) = int x_0^nu_0 x_1^nu_1 cdots x_N^nu_N e^W_lambda/z fracd x_0 wedge d log x_1 wedge cdots wedge dlog x_Nd log v, nuin B \] satisfy the same differential relations as triangle_nu's do. The integration cycle is contained in the torus \(x_0,dots,x_N)in (mathbb C^times)^N+1 \,|\, x_0^-d x_1cdotsx_N = v\ and possibly noncompact, but here we do not try to justify the integral itself. nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:equiv-mirror-int} 
Givental's mirror \cite{Givental:mirrorthm-toric} 
(adapted to a Calabi-Yau hypersurface $X_W$ 
in the weighted projective space $\mathbb P(\underline{w})$) 
gives a solution to the above differential system. 
Let $\mathsf{x}_0,\dots,\mathsf{x}_N$ be mirror $\mathbb C^\times$-variables 
subject to the relation 
\[
\mathsf{x}_0^{-d} \mathsf{x}_1^{w_1} \cdots \mathsf{x}_N^{w_N} = v. 
\]
The mirror potential $\mathsf{W}_\lambda$ is defined by 
\[
\mathsf{W}_\lambda = \mathsf{x}_1 + \cdots + \mathsf{x}_N - \mathsf{x}_0 + 
\lambda\log \mathsf{x}_0. 
\]
Then the integrals 
\[
\mathcal{I}_\nu(v) = \int \mathsf{x}_0^{\nu_0} \mathsf{x}_1^{\nu_1} 
\cdots \mathsf{x}_N^{\nu_N} 
e^{\mathsf{W}_\lambda/z} \frac{\mathsf{d} \mathsf{x}_0 \wedge 
\mathsf{d} \log \mathsf{x}_1 \wedge 
\cdots \wedge \mathsf{d}\log \mathsf{x}_N}{\mathsf{d} \log v}, 
\quad 
\nu\in B 
\]
satisfy the same differential relations 
as $\triangle_\nu$'s do. 
The integration cycle is contained in the torus 
$\{(\mathsf{x}_0,\dots,\mathsf{x}_N)\in (\mathbb C^\times)^{N+1} 
\,|\, \mathsf{x}_0^{-d} \mathsf{x}_1\cdots\mathsf{x}_N = v\}$ and 
possibly noncompact, 
but here we do not try to justify the integral itself.   
The differential relations among $\mathcal{I}_\nu(v)$ 
follow from a formal computation of integration by parts.

nodes.statement: Let F^tw' be the O_M^circtimes mathbb C_ztimes mathbb C_lambda-submodule of F^tw generated by triangle_nu(l), l=0,dots,d-1. First we see that F^tw' = F^tw. We proceed by induction on the degree. The degree zero part (F^tw)_0 is generated by triangle_0 = triangle_nu(0). Hence (F^tw)_0subset F^tw'. Assume by induction that (F^tw)_le 2 ksubset F^tw' for some kge 0. We shall show (F^tw)_le 2 (k+1) subset F^tw'. By Lemma , it suffices to show that zD_vcdot triangle_nu(l) in F^tw' for 0le lle d-1 with delta(l) =k. This follows from Lemma and the induction hypothesis. Therefore F^tw = F^tw'. As we will see in Proposition below, F^tw has d independent solutions. This shows that the generic rank (the rank at the generic point) of F^tw equals d. By the previous paragraph, F^tw is generated by triangle_nu(l), l=0,dots,d-1. Suppose we have a relation sum_l=0^d-1 f_l(v,lambda,z) triangle_nu(l)=0 with f_l in O_M^circtimes mathbb C_lambda times mathbb C_z. Then f_l should vanish at the generic point. Therefore f_l =0. The conclusion follows.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$ be the 
$\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^\circ\times \mathbb C_z\times \mathbb C_\lambda}$-submodule 
of $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ 
generated by $\triangle_{\nu(l)}$, $l=0,\dots,d-1$. 
First we see that $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}' = \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$. 
We proceed by induction on the degree. 
The degree zero part $(\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw})_0$ is 
generated by $\triangle_0 = \triangle_{\nu(0)}$. 
Hence $(\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw})_0\subset \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$. 
Assume by induction that 
$(\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw})_{\le 2 k}\subset \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$ 
for some $k\ge 0$. 
We shall show $(\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw})_{\le 2 (k+1)} \subset \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$. 
By Lemma \ref{lem:generation-over-Rtw}, 
it suffices to show that $zD_v\cdot \triangle_{\nu(l)} \in \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$ 
for $0\le l\le d-1$ with $\delta(l) =k$. 
This follows from Lemma \ref{lem:mult-by-zDv} 
and the induction hypothesis. 
Therefore $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw} = \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}{}'$. 

As we will see in Proposition \ref{pro:basisofsol-cFtw} below, 
$\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ has $d$ independent solutions. 
This shows that the generic rank (the rank at the generic 
point) of $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ equals $d$. 
By the previous paragraph, $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ is generated by 
$\triangle_{\nu(l)}$, $l=0,\dots,d-1$. 
Suppose we have a relation 
$\sum_{l=0}^{d-1} f_l(v,\lambda,z) \triangle_{\nu(l)}=0$ 
with $f_l \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^\circ\times \mathbb C_\lambda \times \mathbb C_z}$. 
Then $f_l$ should vanish at the generic point. 
Therefore $f_l =0$. The conclusion follows.

The \emph{generalized twisted $I$-functions} $I^{{\rm tw},\nu}$, 
$\nu \in B$  are defined as follows 
(the relevant convergence will be shown in Lemma \ref{lem:convergence} 
below):  

(i) In the FJRW side:
\[
I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}(s^0, u, z;\lambda) = 
z e^{s^0/z} 
\sum_{k=\nu_0+1}^{\infty} 
u^k 
\frac{\prod_{j=1}^N 
\prod_{0<b<k q_j + \nu_j, \fracp{b} = \fracp{kq_j}}
(-q_j \lambda - b z) } 
{\prod_{0<b<k-\nu_0 , b\in \mathbb Z} (-bz)} 
\phi_{k-1}
\]
where 
we use the convention of reducing the index $k-1$ 
of $\phi_{k-1}$ modulo $d$. 
This is an $H_{{\operatorname{ext}}}$-valued power series convergent 
on the region $\{|u| < v_{\rm c}^{-1/d}\} \times
\mathbb C_z^\times \times  \mathbb C_\lambda$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{M}} \times \mathbb C_z \times 
\mathbb C_\lambda$. 
Note that, if $k\ge \nu_0 +1$, then 
$kq_j + \nu_j \ge q_j + (q_j \nu_0+ \nu_j) \ge q_j$. 

(ii) In the GW side (cf.\ \cite[Definition 4.5]{Iritani:period}): 
\[
I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}(t^0,v,z;\lambda) 
= z e^{(t^0 + p \log v)/z} 
\sum_{n \in \mathbb Q:  \fracp{n} \in \mathfrak{F}} 
v^n 
\prod_{b=1}^{d n + \nu_0} (d p + \lambda + bz) 
\prod_{i=1}^N 
\frac{\prod_{b\le 0, \fracp{b} = \fracp{w_i n}} 
(w_i p + bz) }
{\prod_{ b\le w_i n - \nu_i, 
\fracp{b} = \fracp{w_in}}(w_i p + bz) } 
\boldsymbol{1}_{\fracp{-n}}. 
\]
This is an $H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w}))$-valued power series convergent 
on the region 
$\{|v| < v_{\rm c}\} \times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda$ in 
$\widehat{\mathcal{M}} \times \mathbb C_z \times \mathbb C_\lambda$. 
Note that the term 
\[
\prod_{i=1}^N 
\frac{\prod_{b\le 0, \fracp{b} = \fracp{w_i n}} 
(w_i p + bz) }
{\prod_{ b\le w_i n - \nu_i, 
\fracp{b} = \fracp{w_in}}(w_i p + bz) } 
\boldsymbol{1}_{\fracp{-n}} 
\]
vanishes if $w_i n - \nu_i <0$ for all $i$ such that 
$w_i n\in \mathbb Z$ (because the factor 
$\prod_{\fracp{w_i n} =0} (w_i p)$ in the numerator 
vanishes on $\mathbb P(\underline{w})_{\fracp{-n}}$ for 
dimensional reason). 
Thus one can assume that there exists 
$i$ such that $w_i n \in \mathbb Z$ and $w_i n - \nu_i\ge 0$. 
In this case we have $q_i(d n+ \nu_0)  
\ge q_i (d n + \nu_0) + \nu_i - w_i n 
= q_i \nu_0 + \nu_i \ge 0$. 
Hence one can assume $d n + \nu_0 \ge 0$ in the 
summation.

Then we have \[ frac\|Box_k+d(z,lambda)\|\|Box_k(z,lambda)\| = fracprod_j=1^N prod_a=0^w_j-1 |q_j lambda + (kq_j + nu_j +a)z| prod_a=0^d-1|(k-nu_0 +a)z|. \] This converges to prod_j=1^N q_j^w_j = v_c as kto infty for a fixed (z,lambda)in mathbb C^times times mathbb C. This implies that the convergence radius of I^tw,nu_FJRW as a power series of u is v_c^-1/d. Similarly, write I^tw,nu_GW(t^0,v,z;lambda) = z e^(t^0+ p log v)/z sum_nin mathbb Q : fracpn in F Diamond_n(z,lambda) with Diamond_n(z,lambda) an element of H_CR(mathbb P(underlinew)). Fix a norm \| cdot \| on H_CR(mathbb P(underlinew)). We have \[ frac\|Diamond_n+1(z,lambda)\|\|Diamond_n(z,lambda)\| le left \| frac prod_a=1^d (dp + lambda + (d n + nu_0+a) z) prod_i=1^N prod_a=1^w_i ( w_i p + (w_i n - nu_i + a)z) right \| \] where in the right-hand side \|cdot\| means the operator norm. Write $I^{{\rm tw}, \nu}_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}(s^0,u,z;\lambda) = z e^{s^0/z} 
\sum_{k=\nu_0+1}^{\infty} u^k \Box_k(z,\lambda)$ with 
$\Box_k(z,\lambda)$ an element of $H_{{\operatorname{ext}}}$. 
Fix a norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $H_{{\operatorname{ext}}}$ such that $\|\phi_{k}\|=1$. 
Then we have 
\[
\frac{\|\Box_{k+d}(z,\lambda)\|}{\|\Box_k(z,\lambda)\|} 
= \frac{\prod_{j=1}^N \prod_{a=0}^{w_j-1} 
|q_j \lambda + (kq_j + \nu_j +a)z|}
{\prod_{a=0}^{d-1}|(k-\nu_0 +a)z|}.  
\]
This converges to $\prod_{j=1}^N q_j^{w_j} = v_{\rm c}$ 
as $k\to \infty$ 
for a fixed $(z,\lambda)\in \mathbb C^\times \times \mathbb C$. 
This implies that the convergence radius of $I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}$ 
as a power series of $u$ is $v_{\rm c}^{-1/d}$.  
Similarly, write $I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}(t^0,v,z;\lambda) = 
z e^{(t^0+ p \log v)/z} \sum_{n\in \mathbb Q : \fracp{n} \in \mathfrak{F}}
\Diamond_n(z,\lambda)$ with $\Diamond_n(z,\lambda)$ 
an element of $H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w}))$.  
Fix a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w}))$. 
We have 
\[
\frac{\|\Diamond_{n+1}(z,\lambda)\|}{\|\Diamond_n(z,\lambda)\|}
\le \left \| 
\frac{
\prod_{a=1}^d (dp + \lambda + (d n + \nu_0+a) z) }
{
\prod_{i=1}^N 
\prod_{a=1}^{w_i} ( w_i p + (w_i n - \nu_i + a)z)
} 
\right \| 
\]
where in the right-hand side $\|\cdot\|$ means the operator norm. 
The right-hand side converges to $d^d/\prod_{i=1}^N w_i^{w_i} = v_{\rm c}^{-1}$ 
as $n\to \infty$ for a fixed $(z,\lambda) \in \mathbb C^\times \times \mathbb C$. 
Hence the convergence radius of 
$I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}(t^0,v,z)$ as a power series of 
$v$ is no less than $v_{\rm c}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{pro:basisofsol-cFtw} 
For each $\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}(\overline{H},\mathbb C)$, 
the map 
\[
I^\varphi \colon \widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw} 
\longrightarrow \mathcal{O}, \quad 
\triangle_\nu \longmapsto z^{-1} \varphi(I^{{\rm tw},\nu}), \quad 
\nu \in B 
\]
defines a solution to the $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}^{\rm tw}$-module 
$\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}$, i.e.\ a homomorphism of 
$\widehat{\mathcal{R}}^{\rm tw}$-modules. 
Moreover, for a $\mathbb C$-basis $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_d$ of 
$\operatorname{Hom}(\overline{H},\mathbb C)$, the corresponding solutions 
$I^{\varphi_1},\dots,I^{\varphi_{d}}$ are linearly independent. 
(In fact, they form a basis of solutions by 
Theorem \ref{thm:cFtw-free}.)

\label{thm:refined-mirrorthm} 
In both FJRW and GW theories, there exist 
$\overline{H}$-valued complex analytic functions 
$\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$, $\nu\in B$ defined 
on an open set $\widehat{U} \times \mathbb C_z\times \mathbb C_\lambda
\subset \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \times \mathbb C_z \times \mathbb C_\lambda$ 
such that 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:Itw-Upsilon}
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(x;\lambda),z;\lambda) I^{{\rm tw},\nu}(x, z;\lambda) 
= z \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}(x,z;\lambda).
\end{equation} 
Here $\varsigma$ denotes the mirror map \eqref{eq:mirrormap} 
in each theory. 
The fundamental solution $L(\varsigma(x;\lambda),z;\lambda)$ is also 
analytic over $\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda$. 
The open subset $\widehat{U}\subset \widehat{\mathcal{M}}$ is of the form $\{|u|<\epsilon\}$ 
for FJRW theory and is of the form $\{|v|<\epsilon\}$ for GW theory.  
For $\nu=0$, we have $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},0} = F\cdot T_0$ 
where $F$ is the function appearing in \eqref{eq:z-asympt-Itw}.

First we discuss the case of FJRW theory. 
By Theorem \ref{thm:FJRW-mirrorthm}, we have 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:Jtw-Itw} 
F(u) J^{{\rm tw}}
(\varsigma(s^0, u;\lambda),z;\lambda ) = I^{{\rm tw}, 0}(s^0, u, z;\lambda) 
\quad \text{for } \ 
s^0 = 0 
\end{equation} 
where the subscripts ``FJRW" are omitted. 
We have $
\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda) = s^0 T_0 + 
\varsigma(0,u;\lambda)$ and 
$I^{{\rm tw},0}(s^0, z;\lambda) = e^{s^0/z} I^{{\rm tw},0}(0,z;\lambda)$. 
By the string equation for the twisted invariants 
(see \S \ref{subsubsec:twistedtheory}), 
we have 
\[
J^{{\rm tw}}(s^0 T_0 + \varsigma(0, u;\lambda), z;\lambda) 
= e^{s^0/z} J^{{\rm tw}}(\varsigma(0, u;\lambda),z;\lambda). 
\]
Hence \eqref{eq:Jtw-Itw} holds for arbitrary $s^0$. 
Therefore, by Proposition \ref{pro:Ltw-Jtw}, we have 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:Upsilon0}
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda) I^{{\rm tw},0}(s^0,u,z;\lambda) 
= z F(u) T_0. 
\end{equation} 
This shows that one can take 
$\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},0}(s^0,u,z;\lambda) = F(u) T_0$. 
The other $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$'s are obtained from 
this by differentiation. 
To see this, we use the fact that the generalized 
$I$-functions satisfy \eqref{eq:diffeq-generalized-I} 
and that we have by Proposition \ref{pro:twisted-fundsol} 
\begin{equation*} 

(\varsigma^*\nabla^{{\rm tw}}_{z D_u}) \circ  
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda) = 
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda) \circ z D_u, 
\end{equation*} 
where $\varsigma^* \nabla^{\rm tw}_{zD_u} = zD_u + 
(D_u \varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda)) \bullet^{\rm tw}$. 
For example, one obtains $z \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},e_i}$ as 
\begin{align*} 
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda) I^{{\rm tw},e_i}(s^0,u,z;\lambda) 
& = L^{\rm tw} (\varsigma(t^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda)  (-q_i z D_u - q_i \lambda) \cdot 
I^{{\rm tw},0}(s^0,u,z;\lambda) \\
& = (-q_i \varsigma^* \nabla^{{\rm tw}}_{z D_u}-q_i\lambda) \left( 
z F(u) T_0 \right).  
\end{align*} 
To obtain $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw}, \nu}$ for a general $\nu$, 
we use the following differential 
operator: 
\[
P_\nu(zD_u) = v^{k} 
\prod_{b=1}^{\nu_0 + kd} (- zD_u + bz) 
\cdot 
\prod_{i=1}^N 
\frac{
\prod_{b=-\infty}^{\nu_i - k w_i -1}(-q_i z D_u - q_i \lambda - b z) } 
{\prod_{b=-\infty}^{-1} (-q_i z D_u - q_i \lambda - b z) } 
\]
where $k$ is an integer such that $\nu_0 + kd \ge 0$. 
When $\nu_i - k w_i < 0$ for some $i$, we expand 
the factor $(-q_i z D_u -q_i \lambda - bz )^{-1}$ 
in the $\lambda^{-1}$-series 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty (-q_i\lambda)^{-n-1} (bz + q_i zD_u)^n.  
\]
Then we have $P_\nu(z D_u) I^{{\rm tw},0} = I^{{\rm tw},\nu}$. 
By applying $P_\nu(\varsigma^* \nabla_{zD_u})$ 
to \eqref{eq:Upsilon0}, one obtains \eqref{eq:Itw-Upsilon}
with $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}(s^0,u;\lambda) = 
P_\nu(\varsigma^*\nabla_{z D_u}) F(u) T_0$. 
Note that this expression makes sense as an element of 
$\overline{H}\otimes \mathbb C[z](\!(\lambda^{-1})\!)[\![s^0,u]\!]$. 
This is because $\varsigma^*\nabla_{zD_u} =z D_u + 
(D_u \varsigma)\bullet^{\rm tw} = z D_u + O(u)$ 
(note that $\varsigma(s^0,u) = s^0 \phi_0 - u \phi_1 + O(u^2)$). 
A posteriori, we know that 
$\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ belongs to 
$\overline{H}\otimes \mathbb C[z,\lambda][\![s^0,u]\!]$ 
by \eqref{eq:Itw-Upsilon} since 
$L^{\rm tw}$, $I^{\rm tw}$ and $\varsigma$ are regular at $\lambda=0$. 

Next we show the analyticity of $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ 
and $L^{{\rm tw}}$. It suffices to show the analyticity of $L^{\rm tw}$. 
By \eqref{eq:Itw-Upsilon} we have 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:Birkhoff} 
z^{-1} 
\begin{bmatrix}
\vert & & \vert \\  
u^{-1} I^{{\rm tw},\nu(0)}& \dots & u^{-d}I^{{\rm tw},\nu(d-1)} \\ 
\vert & & \vert  
\end{bmatrix} 
= 
(L^{\rm tw})^{-1}
\begin{bmatrix} 
\vert &  & \vert \\ 
u^{-1} \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu(0)} & \dots & u^{-d} \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu(d-1)} \\
\vert &  & \vert 
\end{bmatrix} 
\end{equation} 
where $\nu(l)$ is as in Lemma \ref{lem:generation-over-Rtw}. 
Using the basis $\phi_0,\dots,\phi_{d-1}$ of $\overline{H}$, one can 
view this as an equality of $(d,d)$ matrices. 
Write $\gamma(z)$ for the left-hand side. 
It is invertible near $u=0$ 
because of the asymptotics \eqref{eq:FJRW-Itw-asympt}. 
Hence $S^1 \ni z\mapsto \gamma(z)$ 
defines an element of the loop group $LGL_d=C^\infty(S^1,GL_d)$. 
As observed by Coates-Givental \cite{Coates-Givental} and 
Guest \cite{Guest:D-module}, we can regard \eqref{eq:Birkhoff} 
as a Birkhoff factorization  
of $\gamma(z)$ because $(L^{\rm tw})^{-1} = \operatorname{id} + O(z^{-1})$ and 
$\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ is regular at $z=0$. 
Birkhoff's theorem \cite{Pressley-Segal} says that 
the multiplication map 
$L_1^-GL_d \times L^+ GL_d \to LGL_d$ is an isomorphism onto 
an open and dense subset called the ``big cell". 
Here $L_1^- GL_d$ is the subgroup consisting of the boundary values of 
holomorphic maps $\gamma_- \colon 
\{z\in \mathbb C\cup \{\infty\} \mid |z|< 1\} \to GL_d$ 
satisfying $\gamma_-(\infty) =\operatorname{id}$ and 
$L^+GL_d$ is the subgroup consisting of the boundary values of 
holomorphic maps $\gamma_+ \colon 
\{z\in \mathbb C \mid |z|>1\} \to GL_d$. 
The asymptotics \eqref{eq:FJRW-Itw-asympt} 
ensures that $\gamma(z)$ is in the big cell for 
$|u|<\epsilon$ and $|\lambda|\le 1$ for sufficiently 
small $\epsilon>0$. 
Hence its Birkhoff factor $\gamma_-(z) =
L^{{\rm tw}}(\varsigma(s^0,u;\lambda),z;\lambda)^{-1}$ 
is analytic on the region $\{|u|<\epsilon, |z|> 1, |\lambda|<1\}$.  
The homogeneity of $(L^{\rm tw})^{-1}$ implies that 
it is in fact analytic on $\{|u|<\epsilon, z\in \mathbb C^\times, 
\lambda\in \mathbb C\}$. 


For GW theory, the theorem 
follows from the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.6]{Iritani:period}. 
When $\fracp{l/d} \in \mathfrak{F}$, 
the function $I^{{\rm tw},\nu(l)}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}$ coincides with 
$z v^{-l/d} {\mathbf I}_\lambda^{\fracp{l/d}}|_{Q=1}$ there 
and we can take $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu(l)} = v^{l/d} 
\widetilde{\mathbf \Upsilon}_{\fracp{l/d}}|_{Q=1}$ 
in the notation of \emph{loc}.\ \emph{cit}. 
We can get the other $I^{{\rm tw},\nu}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}$ 
from $I^{{\rm tw},\nu(l)}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}$, $\fracp{l/d}\in \mathfrak{F}$ 
by applying differential operators in $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}^{\rm tw}$, 
so the other $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ as well.

\label{cor:anconti-twisted} 
Via the $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}^{\rm tw}$-module $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}$ over $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$, 
the $e_{\mathbb C^\times}$-twisted quantum connections $\nabla^{\rm tw}$ 
of FJRW theory and of GW theory 
are analytically continued to each other. 
More precisely, we have a local trivialization of $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}$ 
over $\widehat{U}_\heartsuit$ 
\begin{align*} 
\operatorname{Mir}_\heartsuit \colon 
\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}|_{\widehat{U}_{\heartsuit} \times \mathbb C_z\times \mathbb C_\lambda} 
& \cong \overline{H}_\heartsuit 
\otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widehat{U}_{\heartsuit} \times \mathbb C_z\times \mathbb C_\lambda}, 
\quad 
\heartsuit = {\operatorname{FJRW}} \text{ or } \operatorname{\text{GW}} \\ 
\triangle_\nu & \longmapsto \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}_\heartsuit  
\end{align*}  
such that, under the trivialization, 
the action of $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}^{{\rm tw}}$ is 
given by the $e_{\mathbb C^\times}$-twisted quantum connection 
\[
z D \longmapsto \varsigma_\heartsuit^* \nabla^{{\rm tw},\heartsuit}_{zD}, \quad 
\text{$D$ is a vector field on $\widehat{U}_{\heartsuit}$,}
\]
where $\varsigma_\heartsuit \colon \widehat{U}_\heartsuit\times \mathbb C_\lambda
\to \overline{H}^{\le 2}_\heartsuit$ 
is the mirror map \eqref{eq:mirrormap} in the respective theory.

By Proposition \ref{pro:basisofsol-cFtw}, 
the generalized twisted $I$-functions 
define an $\overline{H}$-valued solution: 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:I-solution} 
\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}|_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda}
\to \overline{H}\times \mathcal{O}_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda}, \quad 
\triangle_\nu \mapsto z^{-1} I^{{\rm tw},\nu}.  
\end{equation} 
which is an isomorphism (see the asymptotics 
\eqref{eq:FJRW-Itw-asympt}, \eqref{eq:GW-Itw-asympt}). 
On the other hand, the twisted quantum connection 
$\varsigma^* \nabla^{\rm tw}$ 
also has an $\overline{H}$-valued solution 
(Proposition \ref{pro:twisted-fundsol})
\[
L^{\rm tw}(\varsigma(\cdot\,;\lambda), z;\lambda)^{-1} \colon 
(\overline{H}\otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda},
\varsigma^*\nabla^{\rm tw}) \to 
\overline{H}\otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda}, 
\]
which sends $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw}, \nu}$ to $z^{-1} I^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ 
by Theorem \ref{thm:refined-mirrorthm}. This is also an isomorphism. 
Therefore we have an isomorphism $\operatorname{Mir} \colon 
\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}|_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda}\cong 
\overline{H}\otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widehat{U}\times \mathbb C_z^\times \times \mathbb C_\lambda}$ 
such that $\operatorname{Mir}(\triangle_\nu) = \Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$.  
It extends across $z=0$ as $\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu}$ is regular 
at $z=0$. 
Now it suffices to show that 
$\Upsilon^{{\rm tw}, \nu}$, $\nu\in B$ 
generate $\overline{H}$ along $z=0$. 
In the case of FJRW theory, this follows 
from the fact that the factor 
$[u^{-1}\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu(0)},\dots,u^{-d}\Upsilon^{{\rm tw},\nu(d-1)}]$ 
in the Birkhoff factorization \eqref{eq:Birkhoff} 
is invertible at $z=0$.   
The discussion is similar for GW theory.

Note that $\widehat{\Gamma}^{\rm tw}_{\heartsuit}$ is invertible for 
sufficiently small $|\xi|$.  
Therefore $\{\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_\heartsuit(T_i)\}_{i=0}^{d-1}$ forms  
a basis of flat sections for sufficiently small $\xi=\lambda/z$.  
Hence for a fixed such $(z,\lambda)$, 
there exists an invertible linear transformation 
$\mathbb V_l \colon H_{{\operatorname{ext}}} \to H_{\operatorname{\text{CR}}}(\mathbb P(\underline{w}))$ 
such that $\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}(T_i)$ 
is analytically continued to $\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}(\mathbb V_l T_i)$ 
along $\hat{\gamma}_l^{-1}$. 
Because $\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_\heartsuit({\mathfrak{H}}^{\rm tw}_\heartsuit) 
= \operatorname{Mir}_\heartsuit(z \triangle_0)$ \eqref{eq:Hfcn-meaning} 
and $z \triangle_0$ is a global section of $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}$, we have 
\[
({\mathfrak{H}}^{\rm tw}_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}})_{\rm continued} = \mathbb V_l ({\mathfrak{H}}^{\rm tw}_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}). 
\]
Because $z\triangle_0$ is a generator of $\widehat{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm tw}$ 
at the generic point (Lemma \ref{lem:almostgenerate}), 
this relation uniquely determines $\mathbb V_l$ 
for a generic $(z,\lambda)$. 
By \eqref{eq:H-and-U}, we know that $\mathbb V_l = \mathbb U_l^{\rm tw}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
Over $\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z$, 
$\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ is identified with the 
$e$-twisted quantum connection $\nabla^{\rm tw}$ on 
$\overline{H}_\heartsuit \times (\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z) 
\to \widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z$ 
by Corollary \ref{cor:anconti-twisted}. 
By Proposition \ref{pro:noneq-reduction}, 
under the natural projection $\operatorname{pr} \colon \overline{H}
\twoheadrightarrow H'$, the $e$-twisted quantum 
connection projects to the quantum connection 
of the respective theory: 
\begin{align} 
\label{eq:mirrorisom-lambdazero} 
\begin{CD} 
\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}|_{\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z} @>{\cong}>>  
\left( \overline{H}_\heartsuit \otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z}, 

\varsigma_\heartsuit^* \nabla^{\rm tw}
\right)  \\ 
@. @VV{\operatorname{pr}}V \\ 
@. \left( 
H'_\heartsuit \otimes \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \times \mathbb C_z},  
(\operatorname{pr} \circ \varsigma_\heartsuit)^* \nabla\right).   
\end{CD} 
\end{align} 
where $\varsigma_\heartsuit\colon \widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \to \overline{H}^2_\heartsuit$ 
denotes the mirror map 
\eqref{eq:mirrormap} restricted to $\lambda = t^0 =0$. 
Here the meromorphic flat connection $\nabla$ 
on $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ (or $\mathcal{G}$) is given by 
the action of $z D_v\in \mathcal{R}^{\rm tw}|_{\lambda=0}$, i.e.\ 
we define $\nabla_{D_v} := z^{-1} (\text{the action of $zD_v$})$ 
on $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ (or $\mathcal{G}$).  

\vspace{5pt} 
\noindent 
{\bf (Step 1)} 
Let $U_\heartsuit\subset \mathcal{M}^\circ$ be the image of $\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit$ 
under the projection $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^\circ \to \mathcal{M}^\circ$. 
We show that the diagram \eqref{eq:mirrorisom-lambdazero} descends to 
the quotient $\widetilde{U}_\heartsuit \twoheadrightarrow U_\heartsuit$. 
First notice that the Galois symmetry in Propositions 
\ref{pro:Galois-FJRW}, \ref{pro:Galois-GW} extends to 
the twisted theory. The map $G\colon H' \to H'$ there 
is extended to $\overline{H}$ as 
\begin{alignat*}{2}  
G(\phi_k) & = e^{-2\pi\mathtt{i} k/d} \phi_k  
& \quad & \text{for FJRW theory;} \\ 
G(\boldsymbol{1}_f) & = e^{2\pi\mathtt{i} f} \boldsymbol{1}_f - 2\pi\mathtt{i} p 
& & \text{for GW theory}. 
\end{alignat*} 
Then the conclusions of Propositions \ref{pro:Galois-FJRW}, 
\ref{pro:Galois-GW} hold for this $G$ 
(except that we do not have the connection in the $z$-direction
in the twisted theory).

By the flat connection $\nabla$ on $\mathcal{G}$, 
the section of $\operatorname{\mathit{Gr}}(\mathcal{G})$ over $U_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}\times \mathbb C_z^\times$ 
can be extended along any path in $\mathcal{M}^\circ\times \mathbb C_z^\times$.  
We see that the given section of 
$\operatorname{\mathit{Gr}}(\mathcal{G})|_{U_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}\times \mathbb C_z^\times}$ 
is analytically continued to the given section of 
$\operatorname{\mathit{Gr}}(\mathcal{G})|_{U_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}\times \mathbb C_z^\times}$ 
along the path $\gamma_l$ in \S \ref{subsubsec:MB}. 
By considering the $\lambda=0$ limit 
in Proposition \ref{pro:Utw-flatsection}, we know that 
$\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}(\alpha)|_{\lambda=t^0=0}$ 
is analytically continued to 
$\mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}^{\rm tw}(\mathbb U_l^{\rm tw} \alpha)|_{\lambda=t^0=0}$ 
along $\gamma_l^{-1}$, for $\alpha \in \overline{H}_{\operatorname{FJRW}} = H_{\operatorname{ext}}$. 
By \eqref{eq:iota-frf}, the projections of these flat 
sections by $\operatorname{pr}$ are $\mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}(\operatorname{pr}(\alpha))$ 
and $\mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}(\operatorname{pr}(  \lim_{\lambda \to 0}\mathbb U_l^{\rm tw} \alpha) )$. 
Diagrammatically: 
\begin{equation} 
\label{eq:ancont-frf}
\begin{CD}
\mathfrak{f}^{\rm tw}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}(\alpha)\bigr |_{\lambda=t^0=0} 
@>{\text{analytic continuation}}>{\text{along $\gamma_l^{-1}$}}> 
\mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}^{\rm tw}(\mathbb U_l^{\rm tw} \alpha)\bigr |_{\lambda=t^0=0} \\ 
@V{\operatorname{pr}}VV @V{\operatorname{pr}}VV \\
\mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{FJRW}}}(\operatorname{pr}(\alpha))  @. \mathfrak{f}_{\operatorname{_{GW}}}(\mathbb U_l \operatorname{pr}( \alpha) )  
\end{CD} 
\end{equation} 
Here we used the fact (Corollary \ref{cor:Udescends}) 
that there exists a unique operator 
$\mathbb U_l \colon H'_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}} \to H'_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}$ such that 
$\operatorname{pr} \circ (\lim_{\lambda \to 0} \mathbb U^{\rm tw}_l) = \mathbb U_l \circ \operatorname{pr}$. 
The existence of such an operator shows that 
the sections $\operatorname{pr}$ of $\operatorname{\mathit{Gr}}(\mathcal{G})|_{U_{\operatorname{\text{GW}}}\times \mathbb C_z^\times}$ and 
$\operatorname{\mathit{Gr}}(\mathcal{G})|_{U_{{\operatorname{FJRW}}}\times \mathbb C_z^\times}$ coincide under analytic 
continuation along $\gamma_l$. 
Because this holds for all the paths $\gamma_l$ with $l \in \mathbb Z$, 
the conclusion follows.

nodes.raw_latex:
We described the global $D$-module $\mathcal{F}$  
as a quotient of $\mathcal{G} = \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}|_{\lambda=0}$. 
In \cite[Theorem 6.13]{Iritani:period}, 
with the aid of mirror symmetry, 
it was described as a \emph{submodule} of another multi-GKZ system. 
We can translate this result in our setting as follows. 
Define the shift map $S \colon \mathcal{M}^\circ\times \mathbb C_z \times 
\mathbb C_\lambda \to \mathcal{M}^\circ\times \mathbb C_z\times \mathbb C_\lambda$ 
by 
$S(x,z,\lambda) = (x,z,\lambda-z)$. 
Then the map 
\[
\sigma \colon \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw} \to S^* \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}, \quad 
\triangle_\nu \longmapsto S^* \triangle_{\nu+e_0}
\]
is a morphism of $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw}$-modules 
by the relations \eqref{eq:relations-cFtw}. 
This is an isomorphism at the generic point because 
both $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw} \triangle_0$ and $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw} \triangle_{e_0}$ 
equal $\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}$ at the generic point  
(see Lemma \ref{lem:almostgenerate}; the proof there  
applies also to $\mathcal{R}^{\rm tw} \triangle_{e_0}$). 
However, $\sigma$ is not an isomorphism over $\lambda=0$ 
and we have $\mathcal{F} = \operatorname{Im} (\sigma|_{\lambda=0} 
\colon \mathcal{F}^{\rm tw}|_{\lambda=0} \to (S^*\mathcal{F}^{\rm tw})|_{\lambda=0} )$. 
See also \cite{Mann-Mignon}.

Then the map \[ sigma colon F^tw to S^* F^tw, triangle_nu longmapsto S^* triangle_nu+e_0 \] is a morphism of R^tw-modules by the relations . This is an isomorphism at the generic point because both R^tw triangle_0 and R^tw triangle_e_0 equal F^tw at the generic point (see Lemma ; the proof there applies also to R^tw triangle_e_0). By Proposition \ref{pro:Gamma-intstr-properties} 
and \eqref{eq:mirrormap-Galois}, 
the monodromy of flat sections $\mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{E})$ 
around the paths $\gamma_{\operatorname{CY}}$, $\gamma_{\operatorname{LG}}$ 
(Figure \ref{fig:paths_in_M}) 
comes from the autoequivalences $\mathcal{O}(-1)$, $(1)$ 
of $D^b(X_W)$ and $\operatorname{{MF}}^{\rm gr}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}_d}(W)$ 
respectively. 
We already saw in \eqref{eq:ancont-frs} that 
the analytic continuation along $\gamma_l^{-1}$ 
(Figure \ref{fig:ancont-path}) is 
induced by the Orlov equivalence $\Phi_l$. 
Thus the monodromy along $\gamma_{\operatorname{con}}^{-1}$ 
corresponds to the composition $\Phi_0 \circ \Phi_{1}^{-1}$. 
The following proposition shows that the monodromy 
around $\gamma_{\operatorname{con}}^{-1}$ comes from the spherical twist $T_\mathcal{O}$. 

\begin{pro} 
\label{pro:spherical} 
For $E\in D^b(X_W)$ such that ${\rm ch}(E) \in H_{\operatorname{amb}}(X_W)$, 
we have 
$[\Phi_l \Phi_{l+1}^{-1}(E) ] = [T_{\mathcal{O}(l)}(E)]$ 
in the numerical $K$-group.  
\end{pro}
